overview: Dumnonia was an early medieval British kingdom in the south-western peninsula, associated with Devon and Cornwall. Its rulers probably used several centres, including Tintagel. This card follows the map’s 600 to 800 window but also uses earlier evidence from Tintagel’s prosperous fifth to seventh centuries. Those finds illuminate an exceptional coastal settlement, not every household across the kingdom.

periods.title: Tintagel’s prosperous centuries
periods.summary: Imported pottery, glass and buildings reveal a thriving settlement with Mediterranean connections. These approximate dates describe Tintagel, not the kingdom’s whole lifetime.

periods.title: Changing kingdoms in the south-west
periods.summary: West Saxon expansion transformed political authority in Devon while Cornwall emerged as a regional British kingdom. The map’s endpoint does not identify one final conquest.

sections.title: A household on a windy headland

items.text: Tintagel offered steep cliffs, a narrow approach and broad sea views, but it also had fresh water. Some small rectangular buildings contained hearths. The settlement combined an unusually defensible position with the everyday necessities of warmth, cooking and drinking.

Excavators uncovered stone walls, paving and steps on the southern terraces. A thick wall farther east could have supported a building or held back a terrace. Finding a wall is straightforward; deciding exactly what its builders needed it to do takes more work.

Surveys identified roughly a hundred buildings across the headland. Their uses are not all settled: homes, stores and workshops remain possibilities. An impressive settlement plan cannot by itself tell us which room held somebody’s bed or where children spent their days.

sections.title: Dinner travelled, and jars stayed useful

items.text: Fifth- or sixth-century amphora fragments from Tintagel came from Greece. These vessels carried wine and olive oil. Broken jars therefore record journeys across seas as well as the food and drink that wealthy occupants could obtain.

Local slate discs probably closed reused amphorae with the help of beeswax. An imported container could begin another useful life after its original contents were gone. Keeping a good jar was sensible long before anyone had a kitchen cupboard full of them.

A rotary quern from the northern ruins probably belongs to the post-Roman settlement. It ground grain into flour. Fragments of bowls, a stemmed glass and a flask, probably from southern France, reveal a very different part of meals: rare vessels that displayed the occupants’ status.

The 2016 excavation recovered barley, wheat and some oats from post-Roman rubbish deposits. The grains survived because they were charred. Rubbish can be an excellent historical archive, although most people making dinner were probably not thinking about future archaeologists.

Few weed seeds and little chaff accompanied those cereals. Researchers suggested that grain arrived already threshed and cleaned, probably from the surrounding countryside. Preparing food linked the coastal settlement to work on nearby farms.

Some barley had sprouted. That might represent preparation for beer, but the researchers also considered spoiled grain burned for disposal. The same tiny find can fit two different kitchen stories; it cannot settle the menu on its own.

sections.title: A window ledge with homework potential

items.text: A seventh-century slate reused as a window ledge carries the Latin words “viri duo”, meaning “two men”, in English Heritage’s transcription. It also has names, Greek letters and Christian symbols. This is a surviving piece of local writing, not a reconstructed sentence invented for the map.

The lettering combines styles associated with ordinary documents and decorated Gospel books. Specialists interpret it as possible writing practice by someone with scribal training. It supports literacy in a privileged Christian setting, not the claim that every child attended school.

Aldhelm wrote to King Geraint and Dumnonia’s bishops about disagreements over calculating Easter and other church practices. The letter, probably from around the opening of the eighth century, shows a kingdom participating in literate religious debate. A calendar disagreement could reach the king’s desk.

Tintagel’s famous connection with Arthur first appears in Geoffrey of Monmouth’s twelfth-century account, centuries after the early settlement. Archaeological evidence for wealthy occupants does not establish that the legendary king lived there. The real jars, buildings and writing are interesting without a royal autograph.

ending.text: Dumnonia lost territory through West Saxon expansion rather than one securely dated final event. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records war with Geraint in 710 but does not give its outcome; a later writer adds that he fled. Devon became part of Wessex, while a British kingdom continued in Cornwall. The imported 800 cutoff is map coverage, not the disappearance of the region’s people.
